opus-5.5.text:
I think what's so compelling about PowerPlay and POET is that they flip the usual framing of machine learning on its head. Most of what we do is: here's a fixed problem, a fixed dataset or environment, now go optimize. But science doesn't really work like that. A huge part of scientific progress is figuring out which problems are worth asking in the first place. And these systems take that seriously as part of the algorithm itself.

With PowerPlay, Jürgen Schmidhuber's idea was essentially to have a system that continually invents new tasks for itself, specifically the simplest tasks it can't yet solve, and then modifies its solver so that it can solve the new task without forgetting the old ones. So you get this ever-growing repertoire of skills, driven by the system's own notion of what's novel but still learnable. That's a beautiful formalization of curiosity and of incremental discovery.

POET, from Rui Wang, Jeff Clune, Ken Stanley and colleagues, makes this really concrete and visual. You co-evolve environments and agents. The environments get harder, but only in ways the current population can plausibly handle, and crucially you transfer agents between environments. What they found is that solutions to really hard environments often couldn't be reached by optimizing directly on those environments. You needed these stepping stones, these detours through seemingly unrelated problems. That resonates a lot with Ken Stanley's whole argument about objectives being deceptive. If you only chase the target, you often never get there.

And to me that's exactly the structure of scientific discovery. Nobody set out to invent the laser by directly optimizing for barcode scanners. Progress comes from an open-ended accumulation of interesting problems and their solutions, each of which opens up new adjacent possibilities.

So why is it promising now specifically? I think because we finally have the components to scale this idea. Earlier, the space of generated problems was fairly narrow, you know, bipedal walker terrains with a few parameters. Now we have large language models and foundation models that carry a rich prior over what humans find interesting, so they can propose problems, write code for environments, judge novelty, even evaluate solutions. Work like OMNI and OMNI-EPIC, or the AI Scientist line of work, is very much a descendant of this lineage. You use the model as a generator of interesting tasks and as a notion of interestingness, and then you plug that into the PowerPlay or POET style outer loop.

The other piece is that, from an evolutionary optimization perspective, which is where a lot of my own work sits, these systems are really about maintaining diversity and quality at the same time. That's something evolution strategies and quality-diversity methods are naturally good at, and when you combine that with hardware-accelerated simulation in JAX, you can run these open-ended loops at a scale that just wasn't feasible a few years ago.

There are of course open challenges. How do you define interestingness without it collapsing into something trivial or exploitable? How do you keep the system from drifting into problems that are novel but scientifically meaningless? And how do you verify discoveries, especially outside of domains with clean simulators? But I think these are exactly the right questions to be working on. If we want AI that doesn't just solve our problems but helps us find the next ones, some form of open-ended problem-and-solution co-generation like PowerPlay and POET seems like a necessary ingredient.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that excites me about both of those systems is that they take the problem of *what to work on* seriously, rather than treating it as something a human hands down from above. If you look at most of machine learning, we fix a benchmark, we fix a task distribution, and then we optimize like crazy within that. And that's great for making progress on the thing we already decided matters. But it says nothing about where the next interesting question comes from.

PowerPlay, which is Jürgen's idea from around 2011 or so, has this very elegant framing: you have a learner, and the learner continually searches for the simplest problem it cannot yet solve, but that it can learn to solve without forgetting what it already knows. So it's a kind of self-invented curriculum. The agent is both the problem generator and the problem solver, and the only constraint is that each new problem has to be just beyond the current frontier. What I find beautiful about it is that it's essentially formalizing something scientists do intuitively. A good scientist doesn't pick a problem that's trivially solvable, and doesn't pick one that's hopelessly out of reach. They pick the problem that sits right at the edge of what the field can currently do.

POET, from Rui Wang, Jeff Clune, Ken Stanley and others at Uber AI, is the more empirical, open-ended-evolution flavour of the same intuition. You co-evolve environments and agents. Environments that are too easy or too hard get pruned, agents get transferred between environments, and you get these stepping stones where a solution developed for one environment unlocks a completely different one that you couldn't have reached directly. That transfer effect is the part people underappreciate, I think. It's a concrete demonstration that the path to a hard problem often goes through problems that don't look relevant at all.

So why is this a promising direction for science specifically? A couple of reasons. One, the bottleneck in a lot of fields is increasingly not solving a well-posed problem, it's posing the right problem in the first place. If you can automate even a small fraction of that, generating hypotheses, generating experimental setups that are informative given your current model of the world, that's a huge lever. Two, these systems naturally produce diversity. They don't collapse onto a single objective, and in science, the interesting discoveries are very often the ones that weren't on anyone's roadmap. And three, with the capabilities we now have in large models, the "problem generator" half of the loop suddenly has a lot more to work with. You can propose problems in natural language, in code, as simulations, and the solver side can be an LLM-driven agent that writes experiments, runs them, and reads the results.

Now, I want to be honest about the caveats too. PowerPlay in its original form is quite abstract, and getting it to work at scale is hard. POET works in a toy 2D locomotion domain, and scaling the environment generator to something that resembles real science is very much an open question. There's also the issue of grounding. In a simulated environment, you have a perfect oracle for whether the agent solved the task. In science, evaluation is noisy, expensive, and sometimes you only find out years later whether a result was real. So you need a notion of "interestingness" or learning progress that's robust to that.

But as a research programme, I think the core bet is right. Intelligence that only solves problems we give it will always be capped by our imagination. Systems that generate their own problems, and are forced to stay at the edge of their competence, have at least the possibility of surprising us. And surprising us is really what discovery means.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting idea is that discovering the right problems is itself part of intelligence. Usually, in machine learning, we specify a task and then build an algorithm that gets better at solving it. But in science, the question isn’t given to you. You’re also trying to figure out what’s worth asking and what experiment might reveal something new.

PowerPlay and POET make that interaction between problems and solutions explicit. In PowerPlay, you search for a new task that your current solver can’t handle, together with a modification that enables it to solve that task while retaining its previous capabilities. So you’re continually expanding what the system can do.

POET takes a population-based approach: you evolve environments alongside agents that learn to solve them. And a particularly interesting ingredient is transfer. A solution developed in one environment can become a stepping stone for progress in another, where direct optimization might have got stuck.

That’s why I see these systems as promising models for scientific discovery. You’re not just optimizing against a fixed benchmark; you’re investigating how new challenges and new capabilities can emerge together. Of course, generating a difficult task doesn’t automatically mean you’ve discovered a meaningful scientific problem. Connecting that process to experiments and questions we actually care about is still a major challenge. But it gives us a concrete way to study the mechanism.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find exciting is that they don’t assume we already know all the right problems to solve. Usually, in machine learning, we fix a task and then search for a solution. But in science, identifying an interesting question is often as important as answering it.

PowerPlay and POET make that relationship part of the process. In PowerPlay, you search for new tasks that challenge the current solver, then improve the solver while preserving its previous abilities. In POET, you have a population of environments and agents evolving together. And crucially, a solution developed in one environment can transfer to another, where it might enable progress that wouldn’t have been possible by training there directly.

So you get this feedback loop: new problems drive new capabilities, and new capabilities make further problems accessible. That’s a promising model for scientific discovery because the path to a useful result may involve stepping stones whose value we couldn’t have specified in advance. The challenge is making that process produce problems and solutions that are meaningful beyond the system itself.
